unit.title: Perform basic repair to electrical/electronic apparatus

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A hotel in Ocho Rios sends five faulty items to your team's repair bench at once. How should you decide the order of work?
options: Start with whichever item looks easiest
Start with the item in the biggest box
Agree an order with the hotel, safety risks first
Start with the dearest item, so the bill is higher

questions.stem: Your team has never repaired this model of appliance before. Where is the best repair information?
options: The maker's service manual and circuit diagram
A video posted by an unknown person online
The sticker on the outside of the box it came in

questions.stem: Why does a technician ask the customer exactly when and how the fault shows itself?

questions.stem: An electrolytic capacitor on a board has a domed, bulging top. What does this mean?

0 V in both directions
OL (open) in both directions

5 A

options: The fuse was old and simply wore out

The supply voltage was slightly low that day

questions.stem: What is the best way to remove a multi-pin part from a double-sided board?

questions.stem: A copper track on a board is cracked across. What is an acceptable repair?

questions.stem: The exact replacement part is not in stock. Why must any substitute be checked against the data sheet?
options: Substitutes are only allowed on the weekend

options: Leave the area bare so the next repair is easier

questions.stem: An appliance has an electronic speed control. What should you do before an insulation resistance test?
options: Raise the test voltage so the result is clear

questions.stem: The earth continuity test on a repaired Class I appliance reads much higher than expected. What is the likely cause?
options: A loose or corroded earth connection

The tester's battery is fully charged

questions.stem: Which instrument is best for checking electrolytic capacitors while they are still on the board?
options: A two-pole voltage tester
An ESR meter
A clamp meter
A light meter

questions.stem: Why is a function test still needed after the dead tests have passed?
options: Dead tests are only needed for the records

It shows the reported fault is really cured
It uses up the remaining test time

questions.stem: A fan's motor capacitor has failed for the third time in a year. What should you do?
options: Fit another capacitor of the same type again
Fit a capacitor with half the rating this time
Tell the customer that fans always do this
Look for a cause such as heat or a wrong rating

questions.stem: The repair needs a part that takes three weeks to arrive. What should you do?
options: Explain the delay and cost, and ask
Order it and say nothing until it arrives

Return the item without any explanation

questions.stem: Parts cost J$4 500 and labour is 2 hours at J$2 500 an hour. What is the repair cost before GCT?

options: They can be sold to another customer later

questions.stem: What can a Level 3 technician add to the repair record that helps with future repairs?
options: The weather on the day the repair was done
The names of the parts that were not used
The colour of the appliance and its box

questions.stem: A trainee wants to swap parts one by one until the fault goes away. Why should you stop this?
options: It wastes parts and time and may hide the real cause
It is too quick, so the customer pays too little
Trainees are not allowed to touch any parts

questions.stem: How should you check a trainee's soldering on a repaired board?
options: Shake the board and listen for loose parts
Check each joint under a magnifier, then test
Ask the trainee whether the joints are good
Count the joints and compare with the drawing

questions.stem: An item is still under the maker's warranty. What should you do before opening it?
options: Open it at once, as the warranty does not matter
Remove the warranty seal so nobody can tell
Check with the customer first

questions.stem: Why should you wear safety glasses when cutting component leads after soldering?
options: The solder fumes will sting your eyes
The flux can splash when the lead is cut
The board's light is too bright to look at
Cut ends can fly off at speed

questions.stem: At the end of a repair session, what should the team leader check?
options: Irons off, parts stored, bench clear, records done
Only that the repaired items are switched on
That the trainees have taken spare parts home
That the soldering irons are left on for the morning

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters UPS stand for, for the battery unit that keeps a computer running in a power cut?
For a capacitor, what do the letters ESR stand for?
What single resistor value, in ohms, can replace two 470 Ω resistors connected side by side (in parallel)?

What do the letters SMD stand for, for a small part soldered onto the surface of a board?
A ceramic capacitor is marked 473. What is its value in nanofarads?
What is the name of the three-terminal semiconductor switch used in many light dimmers and fan speed controls for AC?
What is the name of the part that keeps a DC output steady at a set value, such as 5 V?
Which letter is marked on a fuse to show that it is the time-delay (slow-blow) type?
Which type of thermistor has a resistance that rises as it gets hotter? Give its three letters.
An appliance has a metal case that is connected to earth through its cord. Which class of appliance is it?

What do the letters DMM stand for, for the meter used to measure voltage, current and resistance?
What is the name of the maker's document that gives a component's ratings and pin connections?
A repair takes 1.5 hours at J$2 800 an hour. What is the labour cost, in J$?

essays.stem: You are put in charge of the Centre's repair bench for a week, with three trainees. Explain how you would organise the intake, the order of work and the records.
essays.modelAnswer: Every item would be booked in on a job card with the customer's name and contact, a description of the item and its serial number, the fault the customer reports, and the condition it arrived in, with a photo. I would tag each item with its job number. I would then look at all the jobs and set an order: anything that is a safety risk or urgent for the customer first, then by the time and parts needed. Items needing parts would be checked early so parts can be ordered. I would match jobs to each trainee's skill and pair a weaker trainee with me on harder jobs. Each job card would record the tests, faults found, parts used, time spent and final tests, and be signed off by me after I check the work. Finished items go to a separate shelf, ready for the instructor's function test and collection.
markingPoints: Books items in on job cards with fault, condition and a tag
Sets priorities: safety and urgency, then time and parts
Checks parts early and orders them
Matches jobs to skills and supervises trainees
Job card records tests, parts, time; checked and signed off; finished items kept apart

essays.stem: A low-voltage board that should give a steady 5 V output is fed from a 12 V current-limited bench supply, but its output is 0 V. Describe a logical way to find the fault using the circuit diagram.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the bench supply is set to 12 V with a low current limit, and that the board's input connector is right way round. With the circuit diagram I would follow the path from input to output. I would look closely at the board for burnt parts, cracked joints or bulged capacitors. Then I would measure voltages to the negative rail at test points: at the input connector, after any fuse or protection diode, at the regulator's input, and at its output. Where the voltage disappears shows the faulty section. For example, 12 V at the regulator input but 0 V at its output points to the regulator or a short on the output side. I would switch off, then use dead tests: check the output rail for a short with the ohms range, and test diodes and the fuse. I would replace the faulty part, power up again with the current limit, check 5 V, and record what I found.
markingPoints: Checks the supply setting, current limit and input polarity
Uses the circuit diagram and a visual inspection
Measures voltages stage by stage to find where the voltage is lost
Uses dead tests (shorts, diodes, fuse) to confirm the faulty part
Replaces the part, retests with current limit, records the fault

essays.stem: The exact replacement for a failed component cannot be found. Explain how you would choose a safe substitute.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first find the data sheet or the service manual for the original part, so I know its ratings. A substitute must do the same job and be at least as good in every rating. For a capacitor that means the same capacitance, a voltage rating the same or higher, a suitable temperature rating and the same type. For a resistor, the same value and a power rating the same or higher. For a semiconductor, the voltage, current and power ratings must be equal or higher, the speed or gain suitable, and the pin order the same, because some equivalents have different pin layouts. The package must fit the board and any heat sink. Where the maker or supplier publishes an approved equivalent, I would use that. For safety parts, such as fuses, thermal cut-outs and mains-rated capacitors, I would only use exact or approved parts. I would record the substitute on the job card.
markingPoints: Finds the original part's ratings from the data sheet or manual
Substitute equal or better in every rating (voltage, current, power, temperature)
Same pin layout and package; fits the board and heat sink
Uses approved equivalents; exact parts only for safety components
Records the substitute on the job card

essays.stem: Explain the dangers of stored charge in electrical and electronic apparatus, and how you would make capacitors safe before working on them.
essays.modelAnswer: Capacitors store energy and can keep a dangerous charge after the apparatus is unplugged. Large capacitors in power supplies, motor capacitors and the high-voltage capacitor in a microwave oven can give a severe or fatal shock, and shorting them can cause a flash, burns or flying metal. After unplugging and waiting the time the maker gives, I would find the capacitor from the circuit diagram and measure the voltage across it with a meter on a suitable range. If any charge remains, I would discharge it with a proper discharge tool that has a resistor, holding the insulated handle, and never with a screwdriver blade. Then I would measure again to confirm it is at zero. Where the maker's instructions say a section, such as a microwave's high-voltage circuit, must only be worked on by a specially trained person, I would refer it.
markingPoints: Explains stored charge and the shock, burn and flash risks
Names typical sources: power supply, motor and microwave capacitors
Waits, then measures the voltage with a meter
Discharges with a resistor discharge tool, never by shorting; re-measures
Refers high-risk sections to specially trained people as the maker says

essays.stem: Describe how you would remove and replace a small surface-mount component on a circuit board without damaging the board.
essays.modelAnswer: I would work at an ESD-safe bench with a wrist strap, good light and a magnifier. I would note the part's position and which way round it goes, and take a photo. I would add a little fresh flux to the joints. For a two-terminal part, I would heat both ends together with a temperature-controlled iron and fine tips or tweezers, or use a hot-air tool set as the maker suggests, then lift the part away gently once the solder melts. I would clean the pads with desoldering braid and flux, taking care not to overheat them or lift them from the board. I would tin one pad lightly, hold the new part in place with tweezers, solder that end, then solder the other end, and reflow the first if needed. Then I would clean off flux and inspect the joints under the magnifier for bridges, poor wetting or a crooked part before testing.
markingPoints: ESD-safe bench, light and magnifier; notes position and direction
Uses flux and suitable heat (fine tips, tweezers or hot air) to remove the part
Cleans pads with braid without lifting them
Tins one pad, places and solders the new part correctly
Cleans and inspects for bridges and poor joints before testing

essays.stem: Compare quick-acting and time-delay fuses. Explain how to choose a replacement fuse, and why a fuse must never be replaced with a larger one or bypassed.
essays.modelAnswer: A quick-acting fuse blows very soon after the current goes above its rating, so it protects sensitive electronics. A time-delay fuse can carry a short surge, such as when a motor starts or a transformer is switched on, without blowing, but still blows on a lasting overload or a short. To choose a replacement I would use the same type, current rating, voltage rating and size as marked on the old fuse, the label or the service manual. If the marking is lost, I would work out the normal current, for example 880 W ÷ 220 V = 4 A, and use the rating the maker gives, often the next size above, such as 5 A. A larger fuse or a bypass would let a fault current flow long enough for cables and parts to overheat, causing fire or shock. A blown fuse means there is a fault, so I would find the cause before fitting a new one.
markingPoints: Quick-acting: blows fast, protects electronics
Time-delay: rides through switch-on surges, still protects
Replacement matches type, current, voltage and size; uses the maker's rating
Shows a calculation of normal current
Explains danger of larger fuse or bypass, and finding the cause first

essays.stem: Explain how you would decide whether an item is worth repairing, and how you would prepare and explain an estimate to the customer.
essays.modelAnswer: After finding the fault, I would list the parts needed with their prices and how long they take to arrive, and estimate the labour time. I would add them up, for example parts J$4 500 plus 2 hours at J$2 500 gives J$9 500, then add GCT at the current rate. I would compare this with the price of a new item of the same quality, and think about the item's age, condition, the chance of other parts failing soon, and safety. If the repair costs close to or more than a new item, or if the item is unsafe or parts are not available, I would advise replacing it. I would explain the estimate to the customer in plain words, give them the choice, and get their approval in writing before starting. If the cost changes during the job, I would contact them again before going on.
markingPoints: Lists parts, prices, lead times and labour
Adds up correctly and adds GCT at the current rate
Compares with replacement, considering age, condition and safety
Explains in plain words and lets the customer decide
Gets written approval and contacts the customer if costs change

essays.stem: Describe how you would supervise a trainee repairing a mains appliance so that the work is safe and of good quality.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work starts, I would check that the trainee understands the job card and the fault, and that the appliance is unplugged with the plug kept in view. I would make sure they know never to work on it while it is connected, and that any capacitors are checked and discharged. I would check their tools and meter are in good order. During the repair I would ask them to explain their plan and their test results, and guide them to a logical method rather than guessing. I would check their work at key points: correct parts, sound joints, wires routed away from hot or moving parts, cord grip and earth connections tight, and all covers and screws refitted. If I saw unsafe practice, I would stop the work at once and explain why. The trainee would do the dead tests while I watch, and the instructor would do the function test on the protected bench. Finally I would check the job card.
markingPoints: Confirms the appliance is unplugged and stored charge dealt with; never worked on connected
Checks tools and meter; asks for a plan and guides a logical method
Checks work at key points: parts, joints, wiring, cord grip, earth, covers
Stops unsafe practice at once and explains
Dead tests watched; function test by the instructor on the protected bench; job card checked

essays.stem: Explain how Jamaica's climate and supply conditions cause faults in electronic apparatus, and what a repair technician can do or advise about them.
essays.modelAnswer: Heat is a main cause of failure. In a hot room, electrolytic capacitors dry out, parts run near their limits and solder joints crack from heating and cooling. Dust blocks vents and fans, making it worse. High humidity and salt air near the coast cause corrosion on contacts, tracks and connectors, which leads to poor connections and leakage. Lightning and power cuts bring surges and spikes when the supply returns, which can damage power supplies. When repairing, I would clean out dust, check fans and vents, look for corrosion and clean or replace affected parts, and choose capacitors with a higher temperature rating where possible. I would advise the customer to keep the item in a ventilated place, away from sea spray, to use surge protection, and to unplug sensitive equipment in a storm or before power returns after a cut.
markingPoints: Heat: dried capacitors, stressed parts, cracked joints; dust blocks cooling
Humidity and salt air: corrosion and poor connections
Lightning, power cuts and surges damage power supplies
Repair actions: clean, check cooling, treat corrosion, higher-rated parts
Advice: ventilation, surge protection, unplug in storms

essays.stem: Describe what a good repair report should contain, and explain why each part is useful to the customer and to future technicians.
essays.modelAnswer: A good report gives the job number, the customer, the item, its model and serial number, and the date. It states the fault the customer reported and the fault actually found, with the root cause where it is known, such as a capacitor that dried out because a vent was blocked. It lists the parts replaced, with part numbers and any substitutes used, and the time spent. It records the tests done after the repair, such as earth continuity and insulation resistance results and the function test, with who did them. It ends with any advice to the customer and any warranty on the repair. The customer can see what they paid for and what to do to avoid the fault again. Future technicians can see the history, spot repeat faults quickly, and know which parts and substitutes were fitted. The report also protects the Centre if there is a dispute.
markingPoints: Identifies the job, customer, item, model, serial number and date
Reported fault, fault found and root cause
Parts replaced, substitutes and time
Test results with who did them; advice and repair warranty
Explains the value to the customer, future technicians and the Centre

practical1.title: Run a repair bench: diagnose, repair and test three faulty appliances
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group three faulty appliances (for example a table fan, an electric iron and a kettle or toaster), each with one or two faults planted, and a job card for each. Act as a small repair shop. First, book each item in, record its condition and the reported fault, and agree the order of work. Choose a leader for each appliance, so that each member leads or co-leads one. Use the maker's information where available, inspect, and find the faults with dead tests only: the appliances stay unplugged and the plugs are kept in view. Work out a cost estimate for each repair using the price list and labour rate the assessor gives, and present it to the assessor, who acts as the customer and approves it. Repair each item with the right parts, then carry out earth continuity (where there is an earth) and insulation resistance tests, and record the results. The instructor carries out the function test on the protected test bench. Complete each job card with the fault, root cause, parts, time and results. Photograph each stage and hand in the job cards and estimates.
materials: Three faulty mains appliances with faults planted by the assessor
Job cards, a price list and a labour rate from the assessor
Replacement parts (thermal fuses, cords, plugs, switches, capacitors) from the store
Multimeter, low-resistance ohmmeter and insulation resistance tester
Screwdrivers, nut drivers, pliers, wire strippers, crimp tool and terminals
photos: The three appliances booked in, with tagged job cards
An appliance opened, unplugged, with the plug in view
A dead test showing the fault on the meter
The cost estimate approved by the assessor
The faulty part beside the new part fitted
The earth continuity and insulation resistance tests being done
checklist: Kept the appliance unplugged throughout and checked capacitors before touching them
Followed a logical fault-finding method, not guessing
Found the fault with the right dead test and named the root cause
Worked out the estimate correctly and explained it clearly to the customer
Fitted parts of the correct type and rating with sound connections and the cord grip tight
Carried out and recorded the dead tests correctly
Led or co-led one appliance, sharing tasks and checking others' work
Completed the job card fully and clearly
safety: No appliance is plugged in during the repair; only the instructor runs it on the protected test bench
Check and discharge capacitors with the proper tool before touching them
Keep fingers clear of fan blades and sharp metal edges
Let heating elements cool before handling, and wear safety glasses

practical2.title: Find and repair component faults on a low-voltage electronic board
practical2.brief: Each pair or trio in the group gets a low-voltage electronic board (for example a 5 V regulated supply with an LED driver or timer stage) fed only from a 12 V current-limited bench supply, with its circuit diagram and two or three faults planted by the assessor (such as a reversed diode, an open resistor, a failed capacitor or a dry joint). As a group, agree a method and a fault report form. Inspect the board under a magnifier, then measure voltages at the test points marked on the diagram with the bench supply on and the current limit set low. Switch off and use dead tests to confirm each faulty part. Choose replacement parts from the store, checking values and ratings against the diagram or data sheet. Desolder the faulty parts and fit the new ones, including at least one surface-mount part if the board has them. Power up again with the current limit, take readings to show the board works, and fill in the fault report. Each member finds and repairs at least one fault while the assessor watches, and checks another member's soldering. Photograph each stage and hand in the fault reports.
materials: Low-voltage electronic boards with planted faults and their circuit diagrams
Digital multimeter (and an ESR meter if available)
Temperature-controlled soldering station, solder, flux, braid and desoldering pump
Fine tweezers, magnifier or lamp with a lens
photos: The ESD-safe bench set up, with the board, diagram and meter
A voltage reading at a test point, with the diagram marked
A dead test that confirms the faulty part
The faulty part removed and the pads cleaned
The new part soldered in, close-up
The board working, with the output reading shown
checklist: Set the bench supply to 12 V with a low current limit and checked polarity
Used the diagram to choose test points and read voltages correctly
Confirmed each fault with a suitable dead test before replacing a part
Chose a replacement with the correct value, rating and direction
Desoldered without lifting pads and made sound, shiny joints
Recorded faults, causes, parts and final readings clearly
safety: Only the 12 V bench supply is used; no mains is connected to any board
Keep the soldering iron in its stand and use fume extraction or good airflow
Wear safety glasses when cutting leads and desoldering
Wear the wrist strap at the ESD bench, and wash your hands after handling solder
